clue.text: It takes a smart one to capture a fury

parts.note: a know-all is called a smart Alec, so the smart one is Alec
taken as written

explanation.surface: Only a clever person could catch one of the mythical avenging spirits.
explanation.walkthrough: A know-all is a 'smart Alec' in British idiom. 'It takes' and 'capture' are only joining words, so the clue is a plain charade despite reading like a container.
explanation.definitionFit: Alecto is one of the three Furies, the avenging goddesses of Greek myth.

clue.text: Sailor, like the knight of old, is digressing

parts.note: AB is an able-bodied seaman
medieval knights who roamed in search of adventure were knights errant

explanation.surface: A seaman behaving like a wandering medieval knight goes off course.
explanation.walkthrough: AB, able seaman, is the usual crossword sailor.
explanation.definitionFit: Aberrant means straying from the normal path, much as a digression wanders from the subject.

clue.text: Brothers seen in distress outside in foreign hair -style

indicators.note: the rearranged letters go around the outside of the abbreviation
letters in distress are troubled and thrown into disorder

parts.note: taken as written
BROS is the usual abbreviation for brothers, as in a firm's name

explanation.surface: Brothers are noticed upset by a hairdo from overseas.
explanation.walkthrough: 'In distress' rearranges SEEN into EN SE, which goes 'outside' BROS. The second 'in' is a link word.
explanation.definitionFit: French for 'like a brush', this is a crew cut with the hair standing up short and stiff.

clue.text: Spinning birds?

parts.note: the word for a song thrush is also the name of a spinning machine used in the cotton industry

explanation.surface: Birds whirling round in the air.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Spinning' looks like flight, but it refers to cotton-spinning machines that share a name with the thrush.
explanation.definitionFit: A throstle is both a song thrush and a machine for spinning wool or cotton thread.

clue.text: Time-piece at fault, when you finish the shift

parts.note: a clock is a piece of equipment that keeps time
out means wrong or mistaken, as a reckoning that is out

explanation.surface: A broken clock at the end of a working shift.
explanation.walkthrough: 'At fault' looks like it describes the clock, but it gives OUT, as in 'your sums are out'.
explanation.definitionFit: Workers register their departure on a time recorder at the end of a shift, so they clock out then.

clue.text: It's the edge when I am in bed abroad

indicators.note: one piece sits inside another, as a person lies in bed

parts.note: lit is French for bed
I'M is the shortened form of I am

explanation.surface: A traveller says being in a foreign bed is the last straw.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Abroad' marks the bed as a French word, and 'in' puts one piece inside the other. 'It's' and 'when' only join.
explanation.definitionFit: A limit is a boundary, the edge beyond which one cannot go.

clue.text: The Shelley family

parts.note: not the poet's relatives but the Roman family at the centre of Shelley's verse tragedy

explanation.surface: The poet Shelley's own relations.
explanation.walkthrough: The family is not Shelley's own but the subject of his 1819 verse drama 'The Cenci', about a noble Roman household.
explanation.definitionFit: Shelley's tragedy is titled after this sixteenth-century Roman noble family.

clue.text: Lucifer had no chance with this literary lady

definitions.text: Lucifer had no chance with this literary lady

parts.words: Lucifer had no chance with this literary lady
parts.note: a lucifer is an old word for a match, and the poet Katherine Philips was known as 'the matchless' one

explanation.surface: Even the Devil could not seduce this woman writer.
explanation.walkthrough: Lucifer suggests the Devil, but a lucifer is a match. The seventeenth-century poet Katherine Philips was called 'the Matchless Orinda', so a match stood no chance.
explanation.definitionFit: This was the pen name of Katherine Philips, the seventeenth-century poet.

clue.text: Roaring boys ?

parts.note: roaring boys were rowdy young bullies of Elizabethan London, but here the roarers are big cats

explanation.surface: Noisy rowdy lads of old London.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Roaring boys' were Jacobean street ruffians; taken literally, the roaring males are big cats.
explanation.definitionFit: The big striped cats are famous for roaring.

clue.text: "And when the west is red With the sunset ——" (Stevenson)

definitions.text: "And when the west is red With the sunset ——" (Stevenson)

parts.words: "And when the west is red With the sunset ——" (Stevenson)
parts.note: a fill-in quotation: the missing word completes the line from Stevenson's poem 'Autumn Fires' in A Child's Garden of Verses

explanation.surface: A line of Robert Louis Stevenson's verse with its last word missing.
explanation.walkthrough: The poem's lines run 'And when the west is red / With the sunset embers'; the answer is the word cut from the quotation.
explanation.definitionFit: Stevenson likens the glowing remains of the sunset to the dying coals of a fire.

clue.text: Bill improving as morning draws to a close?

parts.note: AM is the abbreviation for ante meridiem, before noon
an ending is a drawing to a close, so the phrase gives this word

explanation.surface: A piece of legislation getting better as the morning wears on.
explanation.walkthrough: Read the answer as A.M. ENDING: the morning drawing to a close. The question mark warns that the phrase is split this way.
explanation.definitionFit: A bill that alters and corrects existing legislation is called an amending bill.

clue.text: All a mother needs is a shady hat

parts.note: pan- is the Greek prefix meaning all, as in pan-American
ma is an informal word for mother

explanation.surface: A mother says all she wants is a hat to keep the sun off.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Is' links the wordplay to the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: A panama is a wide-brimmed straw hat worn for shade in hot sun.

clue.text: Radicals who go to grass politically

definitions.meaning: in mathematics a radical is a root, as the square-root sign
politicians appeal to the grass ..., the ordinary members of a party

explanation.definitionFit: Mathematical radicals are square and cube roots, and grass-roots supporters are the rank and file of a political movement.

clue.text: Traitors may get red on the rebound, but it's their loss

parts.note: to attain something is to get or gain it

indicators.note: something on the rebound bounces back, so the colour word is written backwards

parts.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: Traitors may turn red-faced when their plans backfire, and they lose out.
explanation.walkthrough: 'On the rebound' turns the colour backwards to give DER. 'Traitors may' and 'but' only join; traitors are those attainder punished.
explanation.definitionFit: Attainder was the old legal penalty for treason, a forfeiture of the convicted person's land and civil rights.

clue.text: Is Parker's Piece such a feature.?

definitions.text: Is Parker's Piece such a feature

parts.words: Is Parker's Piece such a feature
parts.note: Parker's Piece is a park in Cambridge, but here the piece belongs to Nosey Parker, a busybody, so it is a nose

explanation.surface: Asking whether a well-known green in Cambridge counts as a landmark.
explanation.walkthrough: Parker's Piece is a large open green in Cambridge. Read it instead as the 'piece' of a Nosey Parker, a nosy person: the feature is a nose, so the adjective for such a feature is wanted.
explanation.definitionFit: Anything belonging to the nose, the facial feature, is described with this adjective.

clue.text: Loved a gilded French copper

parts.note: doré is French for gilded
a copper coin is a penny, abbreviated d in old British money

explanation.surface: Fondness for a gold-plated French police officer.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Copper' suggests a policeman, but it is a penny, D in pre-decimal British money (from the Latin denarius).
explanation.definitionFit: To adore someone is to love them dearly, so loved and adored are synonyms in the past tense.

clue.text: Equally essential for a tin or a fête

definitions.text: Equally essential for a tin or a fête

parts.words: Equally essential for a tin or a fête
parts.note: a tin needs a tool to get it open, and a fete needs a celebrity to declare it open

explanation.surface: Something both a can and a village fair cannot do without.
explanation.walkthrough: One word covers both a can-cutting tool and the celebrity who formally starts a fete, a village summer fair.
explanation.definitionFit: A can-cutting gadget and a guest who declares an event started are both called by this word.

clue.text: All about you — in France?

parts.note: the French word for surroundings, used in English for a group of attendants

explanation.surface: Everything around you while you are in France.
explanation.walkthrough: The French word for what surrounds you is used in English for a retinue; 'in France?' hints that the word is borrowed.
explanation.definitionFit: An entourage is the group of attendants that surrounds an important person.

clue.text: Proof that the wheel's progress was non-revolutionary

definitions.text: Proof that the wheel's progress was non-revolutionary

parts.words: Proof that the wheel's progress was non-revolutionary
parts.note: a wheel that slid rather than turned leaves a long streak on the road

explanation.surface: A historian's remark that the invention of the wheel changed nothing.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Non-revolutionary' sounds political, but means the wheel did not revolve: it slid, leaving a streak.
explanation.definitionFit: A tyre that slides without turning leaves a black streak on the road surface.

clue.text: Hamlet's father-image was a racehorse

definitions.meaning: Hamlet compares his dead father to the Titan sun god
a famous English Derby winner of 1933 and later a champion stallion

explanation.definitionFit: Hamlet likens his father to the sun Titan, and a celebrated Derby-winning horse bore the same name.

clue.text: —— me? Never" (Browning)

parts.note: a fill-in quotation: the missing word opens Robert Browning's poem 'Life in a Love'

explanation.surface: A line of Browning's verse with its first word left blank.
explanation.walkthrough: Browning's 'Life in a Love' begins 'Escape me? Never, Beloved!'; the answer is the missing word.
explanation.definitionFit: The poem's lover refuses to let the beloved get away, the sense of the missing verb.

clue.text: Bitter-sweet wine

parts.note: a Hungarian dessert wine from the Tokaj region, sweet with a sharp edge

explanation.surface: A wine that tastes both sharp and sugary.
explanation.definitionFit: This Hungarian dessert wine, made from shrivelled grapes, is famous for its sweetness balanced by acidity.

clue.text: "The brazen —— of war had ceased to roar" (Milton)

definitions.text: "The brazen —— of war had ceased to roar" (Milton)

parts.words: "The brazen —— of war had ceased to roar" (Milton)
parts.note: a fill-in quotation from Milton's Paradise Lost, where the cannon is described as having a brass gullet

explanation.surface: A line of Milton's verse with one word missing.
explanation.walkthrough: In Paradise Lost Milton writes 'the brazen throat of war had ceased to roar', the cannon's mouth pictured as a brass gullet.
explanation.definitionFit: A roar comes from the gullet, so the cannon's mouth is pictured as one.

clue.text: Lemans, oddly enough, for old Cantuar!

definitions.note: Cantuar is the signature of an Archbishop of Canterbury; the definition is a medieval holder of the see

indicators.note: the letters are set out in an odd, strange arrangement

explanation.surface: A remark that Le Mans, strangely, suits an ancient archbishop.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Oddly enough' rearranges LEMANS. Cantuar, short for the Latin for Canterbury, is how its archbishop signs.
explanation.definitionFit: Anselm was Archbishop of Canterbury from 1093 to 1109.

clue.text: The longer let is an obstacle

definitions.text: The longer let is an obstacle

parts.words: The longer let is an obstacle
parts.note: in the legal phrase 'without let or ...', let means an obstacle, and the second word of the pair is the longer one

explanation.surface: A tennis remark that an extended let interrupts play.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Let' suggests tennis, but it is the old word for an impediment, as in British passports' 'without let or hindrance'; the longer partner of 'let' is wanted.
explanation.definitionFit: An obstacle or impediment holds someone back, the meaning of the old word let.

clue.text: Monarch to take all proper measures

definitions.meaning: a king or queen governs a country
a measuring stick is needed to take measurements

explanation.definitionFit: A sovereign governs a realm, and a graduated straight-edge is used for measuring lengths.

clue.text: Poona catastrophe was no go in World War I

definitions.text: no go in World War I

indicators.note: a catastrophe is a disaster that throws the letters into ruin and disorder

explanation.surface: A disaster in the Indian city was a failure during the Great War.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Catastrophe' rearranges POONA. Napoo was soldiers' slang of 1914 to 1918, from French 'il n'y en a plus', meaning finished or no good.
explanation.definitionFit: British soldiers in the trenches used this slang for something finished, gone or useless.

clue.text: It's not proper for one Frenchman appointed

parts.note: un is French for one, the number a Frenchman would say
a payment due is one appointed or scheduled for a time

explanation.surface: A complaint that a single Frenchman was given the post improperly.
explanation.walkthrough: 'For one Frenchman' reads as a man from France but means the French for one, UN.
explanation.definitionFit: Something undue is excessive or unwarranted, which makes it improper.

clue.text: Drinks too much and goes over the edge?

parts.note: over means excessively, as in overdo
a cat laps when it drinks with its tongue

explanation.surface: Someone who drinks too much and loses control.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface pictures a drinker losing control; the wordplay reads the clue's two words in the opposite order, 'laps over', as a bowl spilling.
explanation.definitionFit: When one thing extends beyond the border of another, it overlaps it.

clue.text: Fare for Sarah and foreign friend

parts.note: Sal is a pet form of the name Sarah
ami is French for friend

explanation.surface: Food prepared for a woman called Sarah and her friend from abroad.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Fare' could be a ticket price, but it means food.
explanation.definitionFit: Fare means food served, and this spiced sausage is one item of it.

clue.text: John Gilpin's wedding-day

parts.note: in Cowper's comic ballad of John Gilpin, his wife says their wedding anniversary falls on the next day

explanation.surface: Asking the date of the marriage of the hero of a comic ballad.
explanation.walkthrough: In William Cowper's poem, Mrs Gilpin says 'Tomorrow is our wedding-day', so the day is the one after today.
explanation.definitionFit: The ballad names the anniversary as falling on the day after the one being described.

clue.text: A sharp pull-in, instead of a pull-over ?

parts.note: a jerk is a quick sharp tug
taken as written

explanation.surface: A sharp tug inwards rather than over, like a garment pulled on.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Pull-in' looks like a roadside café, a British transport stop, but splits as a tug plus a short word. A pull-over is a jumper, a knitted sweater.
explanation.definitionFit: A sleeveless close-fitting jacket can be worn in place of a knitted sweater.
